evidence.reference_title: Macular corneal dystrophy type I and type II are caused by distinct mutations in a new sulphotransferase gene.
evidence.snippet: In MCD type I, we identified several mutations that may lead to inactivation of C-GlcNAc6ST within the coding region of CHST6. In MCD type II, we found large deletions and/or replacements caused by homologous recombination in the upstream region of CHST6.

nodes.description: In macular corneal dystrophy, loss-of-function mutations in CHST6 abolish corneal N-acetylglucosamine-6-O-sulfotransferase activity. Keratan sulfate, a major corneal glycosaminoglycan whose sulfation confers water solubility, is left poorly sulfated or unsulfated; the resulting less-soluble proteoglycan accumulates within keratocytes and the stromal matrix, disrupting fibril organization and corneal hydration and producing progressive opacification.

nodes.description: In congenital stromal corneal dystrophy, heterozygous truncating DCN mutations yield a dominant-negative decorin. Decorin normally regulates the diameter and uniform spacing of stromal collagen fibrils; the abnormal protein accumulates and disorganizes the collagen lattice, so the cornea is diffusely cloudy from birth with flake-like stromal opacities.

nodes.description: The unifying lesion of the group is inherited, non-inflammatory deposition of abnormal material within the corneal stroma. The deposited substance differs by form: abnormally sulfated keratan sulfate (macular, CHST6), cholesterol and phospholipid (Schnyder, UBIAD1), disorganized collagen fibrils from defective decorin (congenital stromal, DCN), or mutant TGFBI protein (granular and lattice). In each case the accumulating material progressively disrupts the ordered stromal collagen lattice that is required for corneal transparency.

evidence.snippet: Sequencing analysis disclosed missense, frameshift, and/or protein-truncating mutations in 8 of 10 families with CFD that were studied

nodes.description: In fleck corneal dystrophy, heterozygous frameshift, protein-truncating, missense, or copy-number variants affect PIKFYVE (PIP5K3), a phosphoinositide kinase that regulates sorting and traffic of peripheral endosomes through multivesicular body function. Histologically, affected keratocytes are swollen and vacuolated and contain glycosaminoglycans and complex lipids, which is consistent with defective endosomal sorting and produces discrete dandruff-like and ring-shaped flecks scattered across an otherwise transparent stroma. Reduced kinase activity is inferred from the truncating allele spectrum rather than measured in corneal tissue.

nodes.description: In the granular and lattice (TGFBI-associated) dystrophies, missense mutations in TGFBI produce a misfolded transforming growth factor beta-induced protein (TGFBIp / keratoepithelin) that accumulates as insoluble deposits in the stroma. Deposit morphology is mutation-specific (hyaline in granular type 1, amyloid in lattice, mixed hyaline and amyloid in granular type 2 / Avellino, with the amyloid-forming arm conforming to extracellular amyloid fibril deposition). This arm is curated in depth in the subtype-level entry TGFBI_Corneal_Dystrophies.yaml; it is represented here for completeness of the stromal-dystrophy group.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in the UBIAD1 gene on chromosome short arm 1, region 36, cause Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy.
evidence.snippet: Nonsynonymous mutations in the UBIAD1 gene were detected in six SCCD families, and a potential mutation hot spot was observed at amino acid N102.

nodes.description: In Schnyder corneal dystrophy, mutant UBIAD1 remains bound to HMG-CoA reductase and blocks its sterol-accelerated ER-associated degradation, so reductase accumulates and local cholesterol synthesis is dysregulated. The excess cholesterol and phospholipid are deposited in the corneal stroma (often as crystals), reducing transparency; many patients also have systemic hypercholesterolemia.
